'''Cats''', also called '''domestic cats''' (''Felis catus''), are small, [[carnivore|carnivorous]] (meat eating) [[mammal]]s, of the [[family (biology)|family]] [[Felidae]].<ref name="Linnaeus1758">{{Cite book |last=Linnaeus |first=C. |title=Systema naturae per regna tria naturae: secundum classes, ordines, genera, species, cum characteribus, differentiis, synonymis, locis |location=Holmiae |publisher=Laurentii Salvii |date=1758 |page=42 |chapter=Felis Catus |language=la |volume=1 |edition=Tenth reformed |chapter-url= https://archive.org/details/mobot31753000798865/page/42}}</ref><ref name="MSW3fc">{{MSW3 Wozencraft |id=14000031 |pages=534–535 |heading=Species ''Felis catus''}}</ref><ref>The secret life of cats. 2023. ''National Geographic'' reissue. [can be recommended]</ref> Cats have been [[domestication|domesticated]] (tamed) for nearly 10,000 years.<ref name="9500 years">{{cite web | title = Oldest known pet cat? 9500-year-old burial found on Cyprus | url = http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2004/04/0408_040408_oldestpetcat.html | access-date = 2007-03-06 | date = 2004-04-08 | publisher = National Geographic News | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20220612150738/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/oldest-known-pet-cat-9500-year-old-burial-found-on-cyprus | archive-date = 2022-06-12 | url-status = dead}}</ref> Some of the most popular breeds of this mammal include the [[Siamese cat|Siamese]], [[Japanese Bobtail]], [[Abyssinian cat|Abysinnian]], [[Cornish Rex]], [[American Shorthair]], [[Ragdoll]], [[Aegean cat]], [[Russian Blue]], [[Persian cat|Persian]], [[Manx cat|Manx]], [[Burmese cat|Burmese]], [[Sphynx cat|Sphynx]], and [[British Shorthair|British Shorthair Tabby]].

==Overview==
Domestic cats may be called "house cats" when kept as indoor [[pet]]s.<ref name="Clutton-Brock1999">{{Cite book |title=A Natural History of Domesticated Mammals |last=Clutton-Brock |first=J. |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge, England |date=1999 |isbn=978-0-521-63495-3 |edition=Second |pages=133–140 |chapter=Cats |oclc=39786571 |orig-year=1987 |chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=cgL-EbbB8a0C&pg=PA133}}</ref> They are one of the most popular [[pet]]s in the world. [[Human]]s keep them for hunting mice and rats, and as friends. There are also farm cats, which keep [[Rodent|mice and rats]] away; and [[feral|feral cat]]s, which are domestic cats that live away from humans.<ref name="Liberg_al2014">{{Cite book|title=The domestic cat: the biology of its behaviour|last1=Liberg|first1=O.|last2=Sandell|first2=M.|last3=Pontier|first3=D.|last4=Natoli|first4=E.|date=2000|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780521636483|editor1-last=Turner|editor1-first=D. C.|edition=Second|location=Cambridge|pages=119–147|chapter=Density, spatial organisation and reproductive tactics in the domestic cat and other felids|editor2-last=Bateson|editor2-first=P.|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GgUwg6gU7n4C&pg=PA119|name-list-style=amp}}</ref> In 2021, there were about 220 million pet cats and 480 million feral cats in the world.<ref>{{cite web|date=2021|title=Statistics on cats|url=https://carocat.eu/statistics-on-cats-and-dogs/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225150136/https://carocat.eu/statistics-on-cats-and-dogs/|archive-date=25 February 2021|access-date=15 February 2021|website=carocat.eu}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url={{Google books|plainurl=yes|id=B33gDwAAQBAJ|page=616}}|title=Toxocara and Toxocariasis|last=Rostami|first=A.|date=2020|publisher=Elsevier Science|isbn=9780128209585|editor-last=Bowman|editor-first=D. D.|pages=616|chapter=30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Flatt Osborn|first=Jen|date=23 September 2023|title=How Many Cats Are in the World? A Statistical Overview|url=https://worldanimalfoundation.org/cats/how-many-cats-are-in-the-world/|access-date=26 October 2023|work=WorldAnimalFoundation.org}}</ref>

There are about 92 breeds of cat.<ref name="Driscoll_al2009">{{cite journal |last1=Driscoll |first1=C. A. |last2=Clutton-Brock |first2=J. |last3=Kitchener |first3=A. C. |last4=O'Brien |first4=S. J. |name-list-style=amp |date=2009 |title=The taming of the cat |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_scientific-american_2009-06_300_6/page/68 |journal=Scientific American |volume=300 |issue=6 |pages=68–75 |pmid=19485091 |pmc=5790555 |bibcode=2009SciAm.300f..68D |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0609-68|doi-broken-date=26 July 2026 | issn = 0036-8733}}</ref> Domestic cats are found in shorthair, longhair, and hairless breeds. Cats which are not specific breeds can be referred to as 'domestic shorthair' (DSH) or 'domestic longhair' (DLH).

The word 'cat' is also used for other [[Felidae|felines]], like [[lion]]s, [[tiger]]s, [[leopard]]s, [[jaguar]]s, [[puma]]s, and [[cheetah]]s.

==History==
[[File:Wiki-Felis sylvestris.png|thumb|right|230px|Past range of ''Felis silvestris''.]]

In the past, mostly in [[Egypt]], people kept cats because the cats hunted and ate [[Mouse|mice]] and [[rat]]s in the grain stores. The oldest evidence of cats kept as pets is from the [[Mediterranean]] island of [[Cyprus]], around 7500 BC. [[Ancient Egyptians]] worshiped cats as gods, and often [[mummification|mummified]] them so they could be with their owners "for all of eternity".<ref>{{Cite web|date=2025-04-27|title=Archaeologists discover secret behind why we keep cats as pets|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/archaeology/cats-mummified-pets-egypt-archaeologists-b2740373.html|access-date=2025-05-04|website=The Independent|language=en}}</ref>

Today, people often keep cats as pets. There are also domestic cats which live without being cared for by people. These cats are called "feral cats" or "stray cats". Cats started becoming pets when the ancient Egyptians were around.

==Anatomy==
Cats have [[anatomy]] similar to the other members of the [[genus]] ''[[Felis]]''. The genus has extra lumbar (lower back) and thoracic (chest) [[vertebrae]]. This helps explain why cats are very flexible. Unlike human arms, cat's front paws are attached to the shoulder by free-floating [[clavicle]] bones. These allow cats to pass their body through any space into which they can fit their heads.<ref name="Gillis 2002">{{cite web|title=Cat skeleton|editor-last=Gillis|editor-first=Rick |work=Zoolab: a website for animal biology|publisher=University of Wisconsin|location=La Crosse, WI|date=22 July 2002|url= http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/zoolab/Table_of_Contents/Lab-9b/Cat_Skeleton_1/cat_skeleton_1.htm|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20061206105542/http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/zoolab/Table_of_Contents/Lab-9b/Cat_Skeleton_1/cat_skeleton_1.htm|archive-date=6 December 2006|access-date=7 September 2012}}</ref>

The cat [[skull]], unlike most [[Mammal|mammals]], has very large eye sockets and a powerful jaw.<ref name="Case">{{Cite book|title=The cat: its behavior, nutrition, and health|last=Case|first=Linda P.|year=2003|publisher=Iowa State University Pr|location=Ames, IA|isbn=0-8138-0331-4}}</ref>{{rp|35}} Compared to other felines, domestic cats have narrowly spaced [[canine teeth]]: this is an [[adaptation]] to their preferred prey of small [[rodents]].<ref name=Smith1992>{{Cite book|title=Structure, function and evolution of teeth|last1=Smith|first1=Patricia|last2=Tchernov|first2=Eitan|year=1992|page=217|publisher=Freund Publishing House Ltd.|isbn=965-222-270-4}}</ref> Cats, like dogs, walk directly on their toes, with the bones of their feet making up the lower part of the visible leg.<ref name="Lacquaniti 1999">{{Cite journal|title=Motor patterns in walking|last1=Lacquaniti|first1=F.|last2=Grasso|first2=R.|last3=Zago|first3=M.|journal=News Physiol. Sci.|volume=14|issue=4|pages=168–174|date=1999|doi=10.1152/physiologyonline.1999.14.4.168|pmid=11390844|s2cid=9570415 }}</ref>

Cats walk very precisely. Unlike most mammals, when cats walk, they use a "pacing" gait (walking style); that is, they move the two legs on one side of the body before the legs on the other side. This trait is shared with [[camel]]s and [[giraffe]]s. As a walk speeds up into a [[trot]], a cat's gait will change to be a "[[diagonal]]" gait, similar to that of most other mammals: the diagonally opposite hind and forelegs will move at the same time.<ref name="Christensen 2004">{{Cite book|title=Outwitting cats|last=Christensen|first=Wendy|page=23|publisher=Globe Pequot|year=2004|isbn=1-59228-240-7|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=WmuQQXU6EtAC&pg=PA23}}</ref> Most cats have five [[claw]]s on their front paws, and four on their rear paws.<ref name="Danforth1947">{{Cite journal|title=Heredity of polydactyly in the cat|last=Danforth|first=C.H.|journal=Journal of Heredity|volume=38|pages=107–112|year=1947|url= http://jhered.oxfordjournals.org/content/38/4/107.full.pdf|pmid=20242531|issue=4|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a105701}}</ref> On the inside of the front paws there is something which looks like a sixth "finger". This special feature on the inside of the [[wrist]]s is the carpal pad. The carpal pad is also found on other cats and on dogs.

== Colouring ==
Although cats can have many different colourings, they genetically can only have two coat colours, orange and black. Cats with grey and white fur or markings have a masking [[gene]], but will still have a base of orange or black. 

The gene for colouring is in the [[X chromosome]]. As females have two X chromosomes, they can have two or more colours. It is for this reason that [[Calico cat|calico]] and [[Tortoiseshell cat|tortoiseshell]] cats are mostly female.

==Behaviour==
[[File:Don't mess with me mum!.jpg|thumb|right|200px|The cat in the middle is angry at the cat on the bottom. It is displaying a warning.]]
[[File:Cat November 2010-1a.jpg|thumb|right|200px|The stripes on this standard tabby cat help it hide in long grass and bushes. It's a kind of [[camouflage]].]]

Cats are active [[carnivore]]s, meaning that in the wild they hunt live animals. They mostly hunt small [[mammal]]s (like [[mice]]). They will also sometimes hunt [[bird]]s. Cats eat a wide variety of animals, including [[insect]]s such as flies and grasshoppers.<ref>Pond G. & Dineen J. ''The family library of cats''. London: Octopus, p47.</ref> Their main method of hunting is ''stalk and pounce''. 

The basic cat coat colouring, [[tabby]] (see top photo), makes it easy for the cat to hide in [[grass]] and [[woodland]]. The cat moves towards the animal it wants to hunt, keeping its body flat and near the ground so that it cannot be seen easily. When it is close enough, it runs towards the animal it is hunting and tries to jump on it. Cats, especially kittens, practice these [[instinct]]ive behaviours in play with each other or on small toys.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cat Coat Colours And Patterns {{!}} Choosing The Right Cat For You {{!}} Cats|url=https://www.omlet.co.uk/guide/cats/choosing_the_right_cat_for_you/cat_coat_colours_and_patterns|access-date=2025-05-04|website=www.omlet.co.uk|language=en-gb}}</ref>

Cats can catch fish. They try to flip the fish out of the water and over the cat's shoulders using their front paw. Research showed this to be an [[innate]] (inherited) behaviour pattern which developed early and without the mother teaching it.<ref>Morris D. 1986. ''Catwatching: the essential guide to cat behaviour.'' London: Cape, p72/3.</ref>

Cats are quiet and mostly well-behaved animals, making them popular pets. Young kittens are playful. They can easily entertain themselves with a variety of store-bought or homemade toys. House cats have also been known to teach themselves to use lever-type doorknobs and toilet handles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WofFb_eOxxA|title=Gizmo Flushes|last=Nick Sayer|date=19 April 2006|via=YouTube}}</ref> However, cats are naturally curious, so some domesticated cats may get into some mischief.

Cats are [[wikt:independent|independent]] animals. They can look after themselves and do not need as much attention as dogs do.

===Communication===
{{Anchor|Purr}}

Cats use a wide range of vocal and non-vocal signals for [[communication]]. Vocalizations include [[meow]]ing, [[purr|purring]], trilling, hissing, growling, squeaking, [[chirp]]ing, [[click]]ing, and grunting.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.channel3000.com/news/1472741/detail.html |title=Meows mean more to cat lovers |publisher=Channel3000.com |access-date=14 June 2006 |archive-date=4 August 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030804205624/http://www.channel3000.com/news/1472741/detail.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Adult cats rarely meow at one another but frequently use meowing to communicate with humans, often modifying their vocalizations based on context and response.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=McComb |first1=K. |last2=Taylor |first2=A. M. |last3=Wilson |first3=C. |last4=Charlton |first4=B. D. |date=2015 |title=The Meows of Domestic Cats (''Felis catus''): Honest Signals or Vocal Deception? |journal=Current Biology |volume=25 |issue=17 |pages=2264–2268 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2015.07.048 |pmid=26235649 |pmc=4618611 }}</ref>

Purring is most commonly associated with positive states such as relaxation or social contact, but it also occurs during stress, pain, or illness, suggesting a self-soothing or physiological function.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zambelli |first1=D. |last2=Torri |first2=R. |last3=Prato-Previde |first3=E. |date=2016 |title=The Domestic Cat: The Biology of Its Behaviour |journal=Animal Cognition |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=1041–1051 |doi=10.1007/s10071-016-1007-8 |doi-broken-date=26 July 2026 }}</ref> Trilling and chirping are often used in friendly interactions, particularly between mothers and kittens or during hunting-related excitement.

Feral cats are generally silent toward humans and rely more heavily on body language and scent-based communication than vocal signals.<ref>{{cite book |last=Jensen |first=P. |title=The Ethology of Domestic Animals |url=https://archive.org/details/ethologyofdomest0000unse_p5u8 |publisher=CABI |year=2009 |isbn=9781845935368 |location=Wallingford, England}}</ref>{{rp|208}}

Cats also communicate through [[Body language|body posture]] and facial expressions. Tail position and ear orientation are especially important. An upright tail usually signals friendliness and confidence, while flattened ears indicate fear or aggression.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cafazzo |first1=S. |last2=Natoli |first2=E. |date=2009 |title=The Social Function of Tail Up in the Domestic Cat (''Felis silvestris catus'') |journal=Behavioural Processes |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=60–66 |doi=10.1016/j.beproc.2008.09.008 |pmid=18930121}}</ref> Cats may also perform slow blinking, a behavior interpreted as a friendly or affiliative signal toward humans and other cats.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harper |first1=R. |date=2019 |title=Cats slow blink: A triadic social interaction |journal=Animal Behaviour |volume=156 |pages=13–19 |doi=10.1016/j.anbehav.2019.07.014 |doi-broken-date=26 July 2026 }}</ref> A cat slow blinking is the equivalent of a human smiling.

Tactile communication includes nose-touching during greetings, head rubbing (bunting), and allogrooming, which help reinforce social bonds and group cohesion.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crowell-Davis |first1=S. L. |last2=Curtis |first2=T. M. |last3=Knowles |first3=R. J. |date=2004 |title=Social Organization in the Cat: A Modern Understanding |journal=Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=19–28 |doi=10.1016/j.jfms.2003.09.013 |pmid=15123163 |pmc=10822437 }}</ref>

==Mating==
Cats only mate when the female cat is "in heat". Heat periods happen about every two weeks and last four to six days.<ref name=compendium/> Several male cats may be attracted to a female cat in heat. The males will fight over her, and the winner wins the right to mate. At first, the female will reject the male, but eventually the female will allow the male to mate. The female will utter a loud yowl as the male pulls out of her. This is because a male cat's [[penis]] has a band of about 120-150 backwards-pointing spines, which are about one [[millimeter]] long.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Aronson L.R.|last2=Cooper M.L|year=1967|title=Penile spines of the domestic cat: their endocrine-behavior relations|url=http://www.catcollection.org/files/PenileSpines.pdf|url-status=dead|journal=Anat. Rec.|volume=157|issue=1|pages=71–8|doi=10.1002/ar.1091570111|issn=0003-276X|pmid=6030760|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170620212227/http://www.catcollection.org/files/PenileSpines.pdf|archive-date=2017-06-20|access-date=2009-10-01|s2cid=13070242}}</ref> When the penis is withdrawn, the spines rake the walls of the female's [[vagina]], which is a trigger for [[ovulation]].<ref>Trigger: in the sense of ''an event which starts other events''.</ref> After mating, the female will wash her [[vulva]] thoroughly. If a male attempts to breed with her at this point, the female will attack him. After about 20 to 30 minutes, once the female is finished grooming, the cycle will repeat.<ref name=compendium/>

Because ovulation is not always triggered, females may not get [[pregnant]] by the first cat which mates with them.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wildt|first1=D. E.|last2=Seager|first2=S. W. J.|last3=Chakraborty|first3=P. K.|date=October 1980|title=Effect of copulatory stimuli on incidence of ovulation and on serum luteinizing hormone in the cat*|url=https://academic.oup.com/endo/article-lookup/doi/10.1210/endo-107-4-1212|journal=Endocrinology|language=en|volume=107|issue=4|pages=1212–1217|doi=10.1210/endo-107-4-1212|pmid=7190893 |issn=0013-7227}}</ref> A female cat may mate with more than one cat when she is in heat, and different kittens in a litter may have different fathers.<ref name=compendium>{{cite web |url=http://vlsstore.com/Media/PublicationsArticle/PV_23_12_1049.pdf |title=Prolific cats: the estrous cycle |publisher=Veterinary Learning Systems |access-date=19 June 2009 |archive-date=6 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191206034630/http://vlsstore.com/Media/PublicationsArticle/PV_23_12_1049.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The cycle ceases when the female cat is pregnant.

The [[gestation]] period for cats is about two months, with an average length of 66 days.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Tsutsui T. and Stabenfeldt G.H |title=Biology of ovarian cycles, pregnancy and pseudopregnancy in the domestic cat |journal=J. Reprod. Fertil. Suppl. |volume=47 |pages=29–35 |year=1993|pmid=8229938 |issn=0449-3087}}</ref> The size of a ''litter'' is usually three to five kittens. Kittens are ''[[weaning|weaned]]'' at between six and seven weeks, and cats normally reach sexual maturity at 5–10 months (females) and to 5–7 months (males).<ref name=compendium/> Females can have two to three litters per year, so might have up to 150 kittens in their breeding life of about ten years.<ref name=compendium/>

===Birth and after===
Pregnant females ("queens") deliver their litters by themselves, guided by [[instinct]]. The queen finds the safest place she can. Then she will clean it thoroughly, with her tongue, if necessary. Here she will quietly give birth. She licks the newborn kits clean. In the wild, leaving a scent is risking a dangerous encounter with other animals. The kits are born [[blind]] and with closed eyes. They ''suckle'' on her teats, and sleep a good deal. After two weeks or so, their eyes open. At that stage they have blue eyes, but not the best sight. A bit later, the best developed kit will totter out of the nest. The others follow. They will soon recognize you as a living thing: that is a great moment. At first, they go back to the nest to feed and sleep. After some more days they leave the nest for good, but still they may sleep together in a 'kitten heap'.<ref>''How to look after your cat'': there are two books with this title, as follows. 1. by Colin and Jacqui Hawkins, Walker Books, 1996. 2. by Alan Edwards, Southwater, 2006.</ref>[[File:2006-07-09 katze2.jpg|thumb|220px|Kitten with string]]

Kittens play endlessly. It is how they do their learning. They will play their favourite games, such as 'hide and pounce', with almost anyone or anything. Soft balls on strings are a standard toy; so is a scratching post.

With cats there is a limit to how far you can train them. They are at least as intelligent as dogs, but they are not pack animals. They like to do their own thing, and owners do best by fitting in.<ref>Gallico, Paul. ''The silent miaow: a cat's eye view of Homo sapiens''. Heinemann, London.</ref>

==Grooming==
Cats are very clean animals. They groom themselves by licking their [[fur]]. The cat's tongue can act as a hairbrush and can clean and untangle a cat's fur. Still, owners may buy grooming products to help the cat care for itself. After licking their fur, cats sometimes get hairballs. A hairball is a small amount of fur that is [[vomit]]ed up by animals when it becomes too big. Owners brush their cats to try to prevent a lot of hairballs. 

Cats have four toes on their back feet, while their front feet have five. There are typically 12 [[Whisker|whiskers]] on the right and left side of the cat's face.

==Food==
Many house cats eat food which their owners give them. This food is [[manufacture]]d, and designed to contain the proper [[nutrient]]s for cats. There are many different types of cat food. These come in many different flavors and costs are often very small.

There is moist canned food and also dry cat food which comes in different sized cans or bags and formulas. There are all kinds of formulae. It seems obvious that the food should be mostly meat, as that is most of a cat's natural diet. But remember, when they catch [[Mouse|mice]], they also eat the bones. So there is need for formulas to have more than just meat.

Cats should not be fed a daily diet of dog food. It could make the cat blind, as it has no [[taurine]], which is a nutrient for the eyes that cats cannot make for themselves.

Cats cannot taste sweet foods (with [[sugar]]) because of a [[mutation]] (change) in their ancestors which removed the ability to taste sweet things.

==Health==
[[File:Youngkitten.JPG|thumb|A very young kitten. Its eyes are just open, but it cannot yet see properly.]]In 2023, pet cats lived for around 13 years.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=O'Neill|first1=Dan G|last2=Church|first2=David B|last3=McGreevy|first3=Paul D|last4=Thomson|first4=Peter C|last5=Brodbelt|first5=David C|date=2014|title=Longevity and mortality of cats attending primary care veterinary practices in England|journal=Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery|volume=17|issue=2|pages=125–133|doi=10.1177/1098612X14536176|pmid=24925771|doi-access=free|pmc=10816413 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Montoya|first1=M.|last2=Morrison|first2=J. A.|last3=Arrignon|first3=F.|last4=Spofford|first4=N.|last5=C.|first5=H.|last6=Hours|first6=M.-A.|last7=Biourge|first7=V.|date=2023|title=Life expectancy tables for dogs and cats derived from clinical data|journal=Frontiers in Veterinary Science|volume=10|article-number=1082102|doi=10.3389/fvets.2023.1082102|pmc=9989186|pmid=36896289|doi-access=free}}</ref> This has increased from an average of seven years in the 1980s.<ref name="Kraft19982">{{Cite journal|last=Kraft|first=W.|date=1998|title=Geriatrics in canine and feline internal medicine|journal=European Journal of Medical Research|volume=3|issue=1–2|pages=31–41|pmid=9512965}}</ref>{{rp|33}}<ref name="Nassar 1984">{{Cite journal|last1=Nassar|first1=R.|last2=Mosier|first2=J. E.|last3=Williams|first3=L. W.|date=1984|title=Study of the feline and canine populations in the greater Las Vegas area|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_american-journal-of-veterinary-research_1984-02_45_2/page/282|journal=American Journal of Veterinary Research|volume=45|issue=2|pages=282–287|doi=10.2460/ajvr.1984.45.02.282 |pmid=6711951}}</ref> [[Creme Puff]], the oldest cat that ever lived, died at the age of 38.<ref name="G2010">{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/guinnessworldrec00vari/page/320|title=Guinness World Records|author=Glenday, C.|date=2010|publisher=[[Bantam Books]]|isbn=9780553593372|edition=reprint|page=320|url-access=registration}}</ref>

Cats that roam outside will get [[flea]]s at some time. Cat fleas will not live on people, but fleas will not hesitate to bite anyone nearby. Vets have a good product which they put just behind the cat's upper neck, where it can't be licked off.

Cats kept indoors most of the time are kept from danger from the outside. That is obvious, but its own nature is to be free to wander. 

House cats can become overweight through lack of exercise and over-feeding. When they get ''spayed'' or neutered ("fixed"), they tend to exercise less. If a male cat is not neutered, it develops a disgusting smell. Neutering can also make cats live longer.<ref name="Kraft1998">{{Cite journal|last=Kraft|first=W.|date=1998|title=Geriatrics in canine and feline internal medicine|journal=European Journal of Medical Research|volume=3|issue=1–2|pages=31–41|pmid=9512965}}</ref>

Kittens are sometimes born with unusual traits. Some are serious problems, many of which are similar to human [[Genetic disorder|genetic disorders]]. Others are harmless, like [[polydactyly]]. Most cats have only four to five toes on each paw. Polydactyl cats have six, seven, or sometimes even more. These cats can also be called ''Hemingway cats'' because author [[Ernest Hemingway]] owned cats like these.
